## Chapter 7: From Architecture to Systems Behavior: Memory, Compute, Communication, and Throughput {#sec-ch7}

*Five Resources, Two Operating Modes, One Refusal to Guess*

### Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- Separate weight memory, KV-cache/state memory, activation memory,
  temporary workspace, optimizer state, and communication as distinct
  resource categories, and explain why training and inference have
  different memory profiles.
- Explain why prefill and decode stress hardware differently, and
  distinguish latency, throughput, and goodput.
- Trace the systems consequences (memory, compute, communication,
  implementation complexity) of GQA/MQA, MLA, sliding-window
  attention, MoE, and hybrid recurrent layers.
- State what cannot be inferred about wall-clock performance from
  theoretical FLOPs or an architecture diagram alone.

### Why this matters

Chapters 2 through 6 taught what an architecture *is*. This chapter
asks what that architecture *costs* to run -- and insists on keeping
five different resources (weights, cache/state, activations,
communication, and temporary workspace) separate, since collapsing
them into one number is the most common way a memory or performance
estimate goes wrong. This chapter synthesizes consequences already
implied by chapters 2-6; it is not a training-systems or
inference-serving textbook.

### The resource ledger

No single formula covers every resource a model touches. Weights
persist across both training and inference. Activations, gradients,
and optimizer state exist only during training. The KV-cache or
recurrent state (ch. 3, ch. 6) is request-specific: it grows and
shrinks with which sequences are currently being served, not with the
architecture alone. Temporary kernel workspace is
implementation-dependent -- it varies by serving engine, not by
architecture.

![Six resources, four lifecycles: persistent across training and
inference (weights); training-only (activations, gradients, optimizer
state); request-specific (inference KV/recurrent state); and
implementation-dependent (temporary
workspace).](figures/rendered/fig-memory-state-lifecycle.svg){#fig-memory-state-lifecycle}

| Resource | Logical (architecture) quantity | Measured (runtime) quantity |
|---|---|---|
| Weights | parameter count $\times$ bytes/elem (ch. 2, ch. 5) | allocated model memory (profiler) |
| KV-cache / recurrent state | ch. 3/ch. 6 formula | profiler reading, includes allocator overhead |
| Communication | bytes/step implied by a parallelism strategy | measured network/interconnect traffic |

: A logical estimate and its measured counterpart are never the same number -- allocator overhead, fragmentation, and framework buffers separate them {#tbl-logical-vs-measured}

### Prefill versus decode

Prefill processes every prompt position at once and can expose
substantial parallel matrix work -- it is often compute-heavy. Decode
processes one new position at a time, repeatedly reading the retained
KV-cache or recurrent state -- it is often memory-bandwidth-sensitive,
since a single new token's FLOPs are small relative to the bytes
moved rereading that state. Neither claim is universal: larger batches
raise arithmetic intensity and can shift decode back toward
compute-bound, but they also multiply cache state, and long contexts
increase cache traffic regardless of batch size. Architecture and
serving engine interact -- this chapter states tendencies, not laws.

### Architecture-to-systems consequence map

Every mechanism taught so far trades one resource for a complication
elsewhere -- none improves every column below.

![No mechanism improves every resource dimension. Qualitative markers
only -- no cell is a measurement. The looped-depth row is a
systems-oriented preview: weight sharing across repeated block
applications lowers distinct parameter count, but does not
automatically lower compute (the repeated applications still run) or
cache/state size -- full explanation deferred to
ch. 8.](figures/rendered/fig-architecture-to-consequence-map.svg){#fig-architecture-to-consequence-map}

An auxiliary multi-token-prediction module (a training-time design,
[@src-43]) may itself become an inference-time draft mechanism for
speculative decoding -- a serving technique this workbook does not
teach; both are covered in depth in a future inference workbook, per
this series' own cross-workbook topic roadmap.

### Parallelism, briefly

| Type | Resource pressure addressed | Communication introduced |
|---|---|---|
| Data | replicates computation across data partitions | gradient synchronization |
| Tensor | splits large matrix ops across devices | activation/gradient all-reduce per layer |
| Pipeline | assigns layer ranges to different devices | activations forwarded between stages |
| Expert | distributes routed experts (ch. 5) | token dispatch/combine (all-to-all) |
| Sequence/context | distributes sequence-length computation/state | state exchanged across sequence shards |

: Each type addresses one resource pressure and introduces its own communication shape -- not derived further here; see [@src-10] and a future training workbook {#tbl-parallelism-overview}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"The architecture with fewer theoretical FLOPs must be faster."** It
need not be. Wall-clock performance also depends on arithmetic
intensity, memory traffic, communication, batching, kernel
implementation, scheduling, and hardware utilization -- any one of
which can dominate over raw FLOPs.
:::

### Applied exercise

Model A: dense, GQA ($H_q=32$, $H_{kv}=8$, 32 layers), 7B parameters,
long retained context, high concurrency. Model B: MoE + MLA (64 routed
experts, 8 active, $p_{\text{base}}=2\text{B}$; $d_c=512$,
$d_{\text{rope}}=64$), same context length and concurrency as Model A,
expert weights distributed across devices. Using only ch. 3's and ch.
5's own formulas: (a) which model likely uses less logical cache; (b)
which has more total weight storage; (c) which introduces expert
communication; and (d) why latency cannot be concluded from any of
this without benchmarking.

### Interview lens

*"Given an architecture report, how would you estimate likely serving
bottlenecks, and which conclusions would you refuse to make without
benchmarking?"* A strong answer separates the five resource-ledger
categories, applies the architecture-to-systems consequence map
mechanism by mechanism, and explicitly refuses to predict measured
latency, throughput, or ranking from architecture facts alone.

### Chapter recap

- Five resource categories -- weight memory, cache/state memory,
  activation memory, temporary workspace, and communication -- answer
  different questions; no single formula covers all of them.
- Logical/architectural estimates and measured runtime numbers are
  never the same number.
- Prefill is often compute-heavy; decode is often
  memory-bandwidth-sensitive -- both are tendencies, not universal
  laws, and batching/context length/serving engine all interact with
  them.
- Every mechanism trades one resource dimension for a complication
  elsewhere; looped depth's weight-sharing benefit does not
  automatically reduce compute or cache/state (full treatment: ch. 8).
- An MTP module may become a speculative-decoding draft source, but
  MTP and speculative decoding are not the same thing, and neither is
  taught here.
- Theoretical FLOPs are necessary but not sufficient to predict
  wall-clock performance.
